intro.html: Some things are here and gone: a rainbow, a firefly’s glow, a train passing through town. Others seem to last forever: a stone statue, a deep friendship, a stain that will not wash out. This topic gathers the words writers use for how long things last, and for whether they can change at all.

Here and gone: ephemeral (a very short life), transient and transitory (passing, temporary), fleeting (over in a flash), evanescent (fading from sight). Here to stay: enduring (lasting long), perpetual (never stopping), indelible (cannot be erased). Change: mutable (can change), immutable (cannot).

words.ex: The rainbow was {ephemeral}, gone before Lila could find her camera.
words.ctx: Fame online is often {ephemeral}: a video that millions watch on Monday may be forgotten by Friday.
words.etym: From Greek ephemeros, “lasting only a day”: epi (for) + hemera (day).

mn.cue: a snowman in the noon sun
mn.text: Pip’s snowman stood proud at breakfast; by lunch it was a puddle and a carrot. Its life was {ephemeral}.

scene.alt: A snowman melts into a puddle in the hot sun while a boy in a scarf looks on, dismayed.

words.def: lasting only a short time; staying only briefly
words.ex: The {transient} storm soaked the picnic and moved on within ten minutes.
words.ctx: Most of the town’s summer crowd is {transient}: visitors arrive in June, rent a cottage for a week or two and are gone by September.
words.etym: From Latin transire, “to go across, to pass by”: trans (across) + ire (to go).
words.note: As a noun, a transient is a person who is only passing through a place.

mn.text: The express train roars through the mountain valley, toots once and is gone. Its visit is {transient}: here for a moment, then away.

scene.alt: A boy waves as a train speeds through a mountain valley without stopping.

words.ex: Kai caught a {fleeting} glimpse of the fox before it vanished into the trees.
words.ctx: The sun appeared for only a {fleeting} moment between the clouds, just long enough for the hikers to see the valley below.
words.etym: From the old verb fleet, “to glide away swiftly.”

mn.cue: FLEE-ting: it FLEES before you look
mn.text: Kai turns, and the fox flees into the trees: one flash of orange tail, and it is gone. His look at it was {fleeting}.

scene.alt: A boy points as a fox dashes away into the forest.

words.def: not permanent; lasting only for a time
words.ex: Her disappointment was {transitory}; by dinner she was laughing again.
words.ctx: The town’s gold-rush wealth proved {transitory}: within ten years the mines were empty and most of the grand hotels had closed.
words.etym: From Latin transitorius, “passing,” from transire, “to go across.”

mn.cue: TRANSIT-ory: life at a bus stop
mn.text: Nobody stays long at a bus stop: people wait a few minutes, then ride away in transit. A stay that short is {transitory}.

scene.alt: People hurry onto a bus that is about to leave the bus stop.

words.def: quickly fading from sight or memory
words.ex: The {evanescent} glow of the fireflies flickered across the meadow.
words.ctx: Like breath on a cold window, her smile was {evanescent}: it appeared for an instant and faded before anyone could be sure they had seen it.
words.etym: From Latin evanescere, “to vanish”: e (out) + vanescere (to fade away), from vanus, empty.

mn.cue: e-VANISH-ent: blink, and it is gone
mn.text: Each firefly glows for a moment, then vanishes into the dark before Zoe can point to it. Their light is {evanescent}.

scene.alt: At night a girl with a jar looks for fireflies whose glows fade in and out.

words.ex: Their {enduring} friendship began in kindergarten and is still going strong.
words.ctx: Many songs are popular for a single summer, but this lullaby has proved {enduring}: parents have sung it to their babies for more than two hundred years.
words.etym: From Latin indurare, “to make hard,” from durus, hard, the root of durable.

mn.text: The great stone pyramid has stood through thousands of years of sun and sandstorms, and visitors still come to see it. It is {enduring}.

scene.alt: An old professor points to a great stone pyramid that has stood for thousands of years.

words.ex: The {perpetual} drip of the leaky faucet kept Felix awake all night.
words.ctx: Living beside the waterfall meant {perpetual} noise: day and night, summer and winter, the roar never stopped.

mn.cue: per-PET-ual: a PET whose tail never stops
mn.text: Biscuit the dog wags his tail morning, noon and night; even in his sleep it thumps. His wagging is {perpetual}.

labels.text: per-PET-ual: a PET that never stops

scene.alt: A happy dog wags its tail nonstop while its owner laughs.

words.def: impossible to erase, remove or forget
words.ex: Theo drew on the wall with {indelible} marker, and no amount of scrubbing helped.
words.ctx: Meeting the astronauts left an {indelible} impression on Maya; twenty years later, she could still recall every word they said.
words.etym: From Latin indelebilis: in (not) + delere (to wipe out), the root of delete.

mn.text: Theo’s marker drawing won’t wash off the wall, no matter how hard Dad scrubs: you can’t delete it. The ink is {indelible}.

scene.alt: A dad scrubs hard at marker on the wall while his toddler proudly holds up the marker.

words.ex: Spring weather is {mutable}: sunshine at noon, hail by three.
words.ctx: The rules of the backyard game proved {mutable}; each new player who joined suggested a change, and soon nobody remembered how it had started.
words.etym: From Latin mutabilis, from mutare, “to change.”

mn.text: The octopus turns red, then blue, then sandy brown to match whatever it touches. A creature that changes that easily is {mutable}.

scene.alt: An octopus changes from red to blue.

words.def: never changing; unable to be changed
words.ex: For Grandma, Sunday dinner at five o’clock was an {immutable} rule.
words.ctx: Fashions and slang change every few years, but some things are {immutable}: the sun still rises in the east, just as it did a thousand years ago.

mn.text: Sun, snow, rain or wind, the old stone statue in the square keeps the very same pose year after year. It is {immutable}.

scene.alt: A stone statue stands unchanged while sun, snow and rain come and go around it.

after.cap: Words for time: how long something lasts, and how.

after.html: Short-lived does not mean unimportant: an ephemeral moment (a sunset, a first snowfall) can leave an indelible memory. And mutable/immutable are about change, not time: an immutable law could be brand-new.

items.q: True or false: an immutable rule can be changed whenever the players want.
items.why: False. Immutable means unchangeable: im- (not) + mutable (able to change).

items.q: Twenty years later, Grandpa still remembers every detail of his first ballgame. The day left an ______ memory.
items.why: A memory that cannot be erased or forgotten is indelible.

choices: The mayfly’s ephemeral life lasts barely a day.
The ephemeral mountain has stood for a million years.
Her ephemeral promise to visit every summer lasted fifty years.
items.why: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time, like a mayfly’s single day.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of mutable?
items.why: Mutable means able to change; immutable means unable to change.
